title: Restrictive design
content:
Design of any kind requires empathy. If you’re making it for yourself, it’s a hobby. Everything else is for someone else.

Great designers know who it’s for. And the design is for them, not for the designer.

Annie Jean-Baptiste teaches us about [restrictive design](https://www.anniejeanbaptiste.com/manifesto). This is what happens when the designer fails to identify and recognize who the work is for, and then leaves people out. “Exclusion is a business decision, even when you did not mean to make it.”

Not everything needs to be designed for everyone. But all well-designed experiences and products are designed for _someone_.

Name your people, invite them in and give them what they need.

title: A New Species Emerges From a 9.5 Million-Year-Old Whale Carcass
content:
When a whale dies and sinks to the bottom of the ocean, its carcass becomes a banquet for smaller marine organisms, supplying food for decades. It’s a perfect example of the circle of life—and also a decent way to discover new species able to survive solely because of these so-called whale falls.

In fact, researchers recently found a constellation of new brittle star fossils near a whale fall that dates back some 9.5 million years.

**Read more: “**[**Are Killer Whales Also Cannibals?**](https://nautil.us/are-killer-whales-also-cannibals-1278581)**”**

As described in a newly [published](https://doi.org/10.1127/njgpa/1335) study, researchers first discovered an ancient beaked whale—specifically fossils of a lower jaw and four vertebrae from the same carcass—in the Gram clay pit in southern Denmark, which was once part of the North Sea.

The whale bones were found in 2018, but it’s only just now that the brittle star species has been identified. These slender-armed, distant relatives of starfish have been around for millions of years, but this is thought to be the earliest brittle star to ever be uncovered at a whale fall feast.

While the researchers can’t say for certain that the brittle star turned up for the whale buffet, it seems likely. Other samples collected farther from the whale remains, for instance, had none of the brittle star skeletal plates. “We considered whether currents had simply concentrated the plates around the bones, or whether local chemical conditions had helped preserve them,” study author Ben Thuy said in a [statement](https://www.eurekalert.org/news-releases/1150243). “However, sea-urchin fragments of comparable size and mineral composition occurred in every sample studied. This makes a preservation-only explanation less likely and supports the interpretation that the brittle stars lived on or close to the whale carcass.”

The new species has been named _Ophiura huebnerjenseni_, in honor of Holger Hübner and Thomas Jensen, founders of the Wacken Open Air heavy metal festival in Germany—an event notorious for its muddy conditions, not dissimilar to the mud that this new brittle star has been preserved in for millennia. ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: “Medium Roast, Cream, No Plastic”: New Coffee Cup Coating Protects Against Microplastics
content:
Your paper coffee cup may be harboring a dangerous secret: a thin polyethylene lining. Sure, the plastic coating keeps your cup from getting soggy, but microplastics it sheds may end up in your body. By some [estimates](https://www.recyclingtoday.com/news/paper-coffee-cup-recycling-sorting-pulping-usa/), Americans use roughly 136 million of these disposable cups each day. But because mixing paper and plastic is a recycling no-no, they may all wind up in a landfill. Now help may be on the way, according to a new paper [published](http://dx.doi.org/10.1021/acssuschemeng.6c03064) in _ACS Sustainable Chemistry & Engineering_.

After their testing revealed polyethylene-coated cups experience surface degradation and particle release, a team of chemists from the University of Waterloo decided to make their own waterproof coating. The researchers developed a recipe for a plant-based protective barrier made of cellulose acetate infused with cellulose nanocrystals to provide sturdiness.

**Read more: “**[**How Coffee Affects Your Sex Hormone Levels**](https://nautil.us/how-coffee-affects-your-sex-hormone-levels-1283854)**”**

“Learning how easily some plastic liners can shed particles was eye-opening,” study author Shirley Tang explained in a [statement](https://uwaterloo.ca/news/science/black-coffee-hold-plastic). “The fact that we have created such a high-performance all-cellulose coating that doesn’t rely on conventional plastics is what makes this work particularly exciting because there are so many possibilities.”

The team tested the substance in a variety of conditions and found it was heat-stable in 176-degree Fahrenheit conditions, as well as resistant to strong alcohols, acids, and bases (not that you should be drinking any of those). And because it’s just as plant-based as paper cups, you can toss the whole thing in the recycling bin.

With widespread adoption, it could even save manufacturers some money. “The coating allowed us to use much thinner paper while still achieving the durability needed for beverage containers,” study author Sayan Ganguly explained. “That could reduce the amount of material required to manufacture cups while maintaining performance and lowering costs. These savings could ultimately be passed on to the consumer.”

Let’s hope so. Starbucks isn’t getting any cheaper. ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: Essential Reading in an Era of AI Doomsaying
content:
Are you tired of AI doomsaying? Whether it’s AI researchers and CEOs warning that AI may kill us all (but only after vaporising most of the good jobs), or critics saying that AI will drive us over a climate cliff, doomsaying is everywhere now.

It leaks from our media into everyday conversations, hovers over our sense of the future, haunts our attempts to envision meaningful lives for ourselves and our children, and intrudes upon every peace. For me, whose job is to contemplate technology’s role in futures worth wanting, doomsaying has become like irritating hold music that the whole world is playing.

**Read more: “**[**AI Is the Black Mirror**](https://nautil.us/ai-is-the-black-mirror-1169121)**”**

It’s also a constant battle to keep from playing it _myself_. That’s because today’s AI technologies truly _are_ dangerous: maybe not to all human life, but to human agency and self-understanding, to our relationships with one another, to our ability and will to think for ourselves, and to our prospects of living sustainably together. That’s why I wrote [_The AI Mirror_ (2024)](https://global.oup.com/academic/product/the-ai-mirror-9780197759066). We can’t evade reasonable fears by looking away from them.

But of course, there is a difference between _doomsaying_ and _calls to action_. Doomsaying fosters decision paralysis, apathy, and resignation. Calls to action reawaken our sense of agency, purpose, and moral urgency. Unlike doomsaying, calls to action are grounded not in visions of how a broken world ends, but in visions of how broken worlds are repaired, remade, and carried with love into the future.

In that spirit, here are 10 books, in fiction/nonfiction pairs, that have shared such visions with me. No matter your views about artificial intelligence, they will help you think about the future, and technology, with more love, more courage, and more wisdom than the doomsayers can muster.

[**_Imagining AI: How the World Sees Intelligent Machines_**](https://academic.oup.com/book/46567)**, edited by Stephen Cave and Kanta Dihal (2023)**

If it feels like the whole world is playing the AI doomsaying tune, try a different playlist. Philosopher Stephen Cave and science communicator Kanta Dihal have given us a book that helps us do just that—leave the media party that only Silicon Valley is allowed to DJ, and listen to alternative tracks (essays, in fact) on AI from all over the world. This edited collection quickly breaks the doomspell with a sprawling diversity of visions of AI and the future, from Europe, Latin America, Africa, East and Southeast Asia, including indigenous traditions that know all too well what it is to be assured that the future has no place for you, and to keep living in it anyway.

[**_A Psalm for the Wild-Built_**](https://us.macmillan.com/books/9781250236210/apsalmforthewildbuilt/)**, Becky Chambers (2021)**

The first of two novellas in her beloved _Robot and Monk_ series, Chambers envisions a future where humans have made all the worst mistakes with machines, and still invented ways to keep on living. It’s a beautiful, contemplative, and pastoral vision of a different kind of future, one where humans and machines have finally acquired the wisdom to know when to stop, and are mustering the courage to make a new start.

[**_More Everything Forever: AI Overlords, Space Empires, and Silicon Valley's Crusade to Control the Fate of Humanity_**](https://basicbooks.uk/titles/adam-becker/more-everything-forever/9781399827904/)**by Adam Becker (2025)**

This is one of many excellent books to yank back the curtain on Silicon Valley’s apocalyptic and messianic fantasies, exposing their roots in Big Tech’s increasingly fetid stew of authoritarian politics and antihumanist ideologies. What made it stand out for me were journalist and astrophysicist Becker’s reflections on his own _Star Trek-_ fueled, childhood faith in tech as something that _delivers_ the future to us. As a sci-fi and tech-obsessed kid of the 70s, who imagined the spectre of a first-strike ICBM in every meteor trail, I too spent years waiting for machines to either consume the world or spirit us away to the stars. Becker’s moving final chapter marks the path that leads us beyond childlike waiting, and toward the tomorrows we can at any time start to build.

[**_The Fifth Season_**](https://www.hachettebookgroup.com/titles/n-k-jemisin/the-fifth-season/9780316229296/)**_,_****N.K. Jemisin (2015)**

AI isn’t actually a theme of the first novel in Jemisin’s triple Hugo Award-winning _Broken Earth_ trilogy. Yet this book, and the series as a whole, profoundly shaped my thinking about technology, power, and the fear of apocalypse. It’s more than a demonstration of Jemisin’s truly astonishing talent of world-building. It’s a reflection on what it means to believe that you can _end_ worlds, how radically that thought changes us, and what happens when world-bending power is controlled by elite castes, or wielded by broken souls. It’s about how people find a way to walk into the future together even as they confront a world coming apart at the seams (here, quite literally).

[**_Prophecy: Prediction, Power, and the Fight for the Future, from Ancient Oracles to AI_**](https://www.penguinrandomhouse.com/books/759692/prophecy-by-carissa-veliz/)**, by Carissa Véliz (2026)**

_Prophecy_ is a look at the long history of human claims to see the future, from religious divination to astrology, from predictive algorithms to mathematical estimates of our AI (p)doom. Véliz gives us an eagle-eye view of the history and politics of prophecy and our susceptibility to its allure. Most importantly it offers a vital lesson: Many claims to know what _will_ happen are concealed instructions to us to _let_ it happen. Ask yourself who benefits from a future where AI has usurped all of your power and liberty, and you may see how a prophecy of AI doom is designed to enlist you in the service of its fulfilment.

[**_Erewhon_**](https://www.penguin.co.uk/books/33951/erewhon-by-samuel-butler-edited-with-an-introduction-by-peter-mudford/9780140430578)**, by Samuel Butler (1872)**

How could a satirical expose of Victorian society written more than 150 years ago, long before the dawn of computing, possibly help us grapple with the 21st century spectre of AI doom? Sit down with Chapters 23-25, which tell a story within the story: ‘The Book of the Machines.’ It’s a story that will sound shockingly familiar, a welcome reminder that our fears of becoming enslaved by intelligent machines—and nearly every detail of the “AI takeover” scenario—have been haunting us since well before the dawn of the computer, when the most frightening technology we could imagine was steam-power. Perhaps, then, we should treat its fears as more confession than prophecy.

[**_Imagination: A Manifesto_**](https://wwnorton.com/books/9781324020974)**, by Ruha Benjamin (2025)**

In _Imagination,_ MacArthur Fellow Benjamin reminds us that if we feel hopelessly trapped in Big Tech’s narrative, haunted by the same fearful visions spoon-fed to us by the same unaccountable powers, we must ask: _What other stories could we write for ourselves?_ She offers a powerful set of tools for liberating human political and technological imagination from the AI doom loop, reawakening an ability that we have never fully lost—to invent new visions of the future that work like open doors, not cages.

[**_The Lathe of Heaven_**](https://www.simonandschuster.com/books/The-Lathe-Of-Heaven/Ursula-K-Le-Guin/9781668017401)**, by Ursula K. Le Guin (1971)**

Le Guin famously rejected the idea of science fiction as prediction, and the stale binaries of utopia and dystopia, often mirror images of the same limited view. Nor did she write about futures with AI or robots. What opens human futures, she argued in her 2002 lecture “Operating Instructions,” is not technology but imagination. _Lathe of Heaven,_ her classic novel about a man whose dreams bend reality, still has much to teach us about the folly and limited imagination of today’s AI leaders, who strive in vain to force the future into the mold of their own utopian dreams, while leaking their dystopian nightmares into our reality.

[**_Vaporware, Inc: How Silicon Valley Sells the Future to Control the Present_**](https://wwnorton.com/books/9781324106319)**, by David Karpf****(2027)**

This forthcoming book offers a compelling exposé of the decades-old con that is “digital futurism.” Again and again, Silicon Valley sells us visions of future abundance and ease that somehow never arrive, like a friend who keeps inviting you out to a free lunch and then doing a runner when the check comes. It’s a bracing takedown of empty techno-utopian promises, yet an equally powerful antidote to doomsaying. Our future isn’t secure, but it isn’t _lost_ either. When the spell of digital futurism breaks, the future is always still in our hands, waiting for us to shape it._Vaporware_ isn’t a book for pessimists, but for pragmatists _with work to do_. As Karpf puts it, it’s “a book for worriers and for planners.” That’s a book for me. Maybe you too.

[**_The Diamond Age: Or, A Young Lady’s Illustrated Primer_**](https://www.penguin.co.uk/books/24031/the-diamond-age-by-neal-stephenson/9780241953198)**, by Neal Stephenson (1995)**

Stephenson was long seen by many Silicon Valley founders as a prophet of digital futurism. His 1992 novel _Snow Crash_ was celebrated for decades as foreseeing the inevitable shift of our lives into a virtual Metaverse. Yet it’s 2026, and multiple costly attempts to force the Metaverse prophecy into commercial reality have gone bust. It’s a reminder of Le Guin’s warning to read fiction not as prophecy, which narrows our vision of the future, but as a mind-stretcher to widen it. So skip _Snow Crash,_ and take a tour through Stephenson’s sweeping tale of a far weirder future, one with a nanotech-fueled economy, geopolitics remade by tribal clashes between neo-Victorian and neo-Confucian revivals, and an AI-enabled personal tutor that might shape a child into a dull conformist or a world-breaking revolutionary. It’s a dizzying vision that defies utopian and dystopian tropes, and imagines AI as a conduit for human agency, love and resistance, not their replacement. ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: Did Life Begin in an RNA World?
content:
Some believe the earliest life emerged from self-copying molecules that could mutate and even evolve. But that may not have been enough.

## Introduction

_This explainer is part of_ Quanta Magazine _’s Origins of Life Week. Check back throughout the week for more stories about one of science’s biggest unknowns._

T here’s scarcely any corner of Earth in which life hasn’t gained a foothold. Living organisms shape the clouds, the climate, even the rocks. But how life first appeared on a barren planet some 4 billion years ago remains one of the biggest questions for science. Many researchers believe that self-replication — an ability to reliably store and copy genetic information — is life’s most core ability. If that’s true, then the earliest life-forms would presumably have needed the sorts of biomolecules that life uses to store and copy genetic information today.

The DNA molecule is the star of this process; it encodes the forms of the protein molecules that enable chemical reactions in cells. To translate the genetic information in DNA into the chemical structure of proteins, cells use RNA. The trouble is, in modern cells, proteins are involved in every step of this process: They duplicate DNA when cells divide, they transcribe DNA into RNA, and they help to use RNA for making more proteins. This creates a chicken-and-egg problem: Useful proteins can’t be made in cells without DNA, but proteins are needed to make DNA in the first place.

A discovery about RNA in the late 1980s seemed to break the deadlock. Researchers found that, in addition to helping to convert genetic information into proteins, some RNAs can act as catalysts that enable chemical reactions. These were christened ribozymes, in reference to the protein catalysts called enzymes. The existence of ribozymes suggested that RNA can both carry genetic sequence information and act as a catalyst, thereby doing the jobs of both DNA and proteins. That makes it plausible that in its very earliest days, life — or the complex chemistry that preceded it — was all about RNA. According to this picture, championed by the physicist-turned-biologist [Walter Gilbert (opens a new tab)](https://doi.org/10.1038/319618a0), life began as an RNA world.

Imagine then that, somewhere on the prebiotic Earth, individual nucleotide molecules appeared and joined together spontaneously and randomly in chains. By chance one momentous day, one of these nucleotide chains acquired the right sequence to act as a ribozyme with the ability to help other RNAs form. Such a prebiotic ribozyme could even act as an autocatalyst, able to replicate itself. In 1996, this theory got a boost when researchers created a ribozyme that could indeed stitch individual nucleotides together to form RNA. This raised the prospect of RNA that could replicate.

Because such replication would be vulnerable to the random noise of the molecular world, errors would happen. Some replicated RNA would have a slightly different sequence from its parent. With such mutations, Darwinian evolution becomes possible: Natural selection would favor mutant replicators that make copies at a faster rate.

These primitive, evolving molecular systems wouldn’t be “alive” in themselves. It’s easy to imagine, however, how some RNA molecules could evolve into forms that catalyzed metabolic processes or made other complex biomolecules — and from there the path to the first truly living protocells comes into view.

The “RNA world,” as the idea was dubbed, sounds good in theory. But there are problems with the hypothesis. In 2019, the RNA biologist [Gerald Joyce (opens a new tab)](https://www.salk.edu/scientist/gerald-joyce/) of the Salk Institute and his colleagues were exploring a method for making new ribozymes in the lab. They started by creating synthetic ribozymes that could make other RNAs. Then they scrambled the ribozymes’ sequences a bit to let them evolve artificially. Although they eventually found a ribozyme capable of synthesizing the RNA from which it had “evolved,” Joyce and colleagues found that the mutations introduced in each round of evolution tended to kill off the catalytic behavior. Very few mutants in each successive generation retained the ability to construct other RNA molecules at all. All told, the experiments suggest that self-sustaining RNA evolution appears to be hard.

What’s more, all of Joyce’s ribozymes were big, comprising perhaps several hundred or so linked nucleotides. However, current experiments have only yielded spontaneous assembly of RNAs that are relatively tiny — about 10 to 15 nucleotides long. It’s big jump to go from random assembly of small, fragmentary RNAs to an RNA world in which large molecules can form, much less replicate and evolve. The chance of functional molecules like these assembling at random and then sustaining themselves in some primordial pool seems minuscule.

But RNA-world true believers have some reason to maintain hope. Recent work from the biologist [Philipp Holliger (opens a new tab)](https://mrclmb.ac.uk/research-leaders/philipp-holliger/) at the MRC Laboratory of Molecular Biology in the United Kingdom and his colleagues has shown that self-replicating RNAs [don’t have to be as big (opens a new tab)](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.adt2760) as Joyce’s ribozymes. In their own RNA artificial evolution experiments, Holliger’s team looked for catalytic activity in small RNAs (between 20 and 40 nucleotides in length), allowing for small changes in length in each cycle of mutation. They found a 45-nucleotide molecule that they christened QT45 (“quite tiny”) that could seize another RNA strand and copy it. “In principle it can copy any sequence,” Holliger said. And getting a 45-nucleotide molecule spontaneously “does not seem an unreasonable ask,” he added. In fact, the researchers say, the catalytic activity might be sustained even if QT45 is split into two fragments, since the parts should remain able to do their jobs.

The researchers also found two other comparably small RNAs with similar activity within a starting pool of around 10 trillion different molecules. Given that this many molecules includes just a hundred-billionth of all the possible RNA sequences of this length, that’s actually a pretty good hit rate, Holliger said. It suggests that this sort of self-copying ability in small RNAs might be common enough that such molecules could have appeared quite readily among random RNAs in some kind of primordial soup.

That “could” is doing a lot of work. It’s not known whether there was a niche for an RNA world, either geographically or temporally, on the early Earth. Holliger and colleagues have shown that rounds of RNA replication leading to exponential growth can be driven by cyclic changes in acidity coupled with cycles of freezing and thawing of the solution — a plausible scenario at the icy poles of the young Earth. But any potential habitat would have to have been life-friendly for long enough for a spark of life to catch.

Perhaps most importantly, it’s not clear that an RNA world would be truly alive. Life isn’t just about self-replicating carriers of genetic information — it takes more ingredients, in particular the existence of some form of metabolism to harvest energy from the environment and use it to make useful molecules. However life started, it probably needed more than just a string of nucleotides.

title: Carl Sagan on How to Live with the Unknown
content:
[![Image 1: Carl Sagan on How to Live with the Unknown](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2018/03/conversationswithcarlsagan.jpg?fit=320%2C495&ssl=1)](https://www.amazon.com/Conversations-Carl-Sagan-Literary/dp/1578067367/braipick-20)

In our recent [_On Being_ conversation](https://onbeing.org/programs/maria-popova-natalie-batalha-cosmic-imagining-civic-pondering-mar2018), NASA astrophysicist and exoplanet researcher Natalie Batalha said something that stopped me up short: as sentient beings endowed with awareness, we are “the universe itself becoming aware.” Echoing poet Diane Ackerman’s lovely notion of [“the plain everythingness of everything, in cahoots with the everythingness of everything else,”](https://www.themarginalian.org/2013/02/19/diane-ackerman-the-planets-a-cosmic-pastoral/) Dr. Batalha added: _“It took 13.7 billion years for the atoms to come together to create the portal to the universe which is my physical self. So in that statement is this idea, or the fluidity of time and space. And I kind of see it all at once. And I don’t know what ‘me’ is. I just feel part of everything. And I feel such deep gratitude for being able to take this conscious look at the universe — at myself as being part of the universe.”_

The sentiment reminded me of a beautiful interview **Carl Sagan** (November 9, 1934–December 20, 1996) gave shortly after the premiere of his epoch-making documentary _Cosmos_, later included in [**_Conversations with Carl Sagan_**](https://www.amazon.com/Conversations-Carl-Sagan-Literary/dp/1578067367/braipick-20) ([_public library_](http://www.worldcat.org/title/conversations-with-carl-sagan/oclc/60375648&referer=brief_results)).

In late August of 1980 — two years after he conducted [Susan Sontag’s most dimensional interview](https://www.themarginalian.org/2013/12/03/susan-sontag-stereotypes-polarities/) and nine years before his [magnificent conversation with Leonard Bernstein](https://www.themarginalian.org/2016/10/03/dinner-with-lenny-leonard-bernstein-jonathan-cott/) — interlocutor extraordinaire [Jonathan Cott](https://www.themarginalian.org/tag/jonathan-cott) visited Sagan’s home in Los Angeles to interview him for _Rolling Stone_. In the soaring the conversation that followed, Sagan stepped into his native nexus of the scientific and the poetic to contemplate our understanding of the universe and of ourselves, the nature of reality and of human knowledge, and how to live with the unknown.

[![Image 2](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2018/03/carlsagan_galaxy1.jpg?resize=680%2C975&ssl=1)](https://www.amazon.com/Conversations-Carl-Sagan-Literary/dp/1578067367/braipick-20)

Carl Sagan

Sagan tells Cott:

> It’s a critical moment in the history of the world… We are the representatives of the cosmos; we are an example of what hydrogen atoms can do, given fifteen billion years of cosmic evolution. And we resonate to these questions. We start with the origin of every human being, and then the origin of our community, our nation, the human species, who our ancestors were and then the riddle of the origin of life. And the questions: where did the Earth and Solar System come from? Where did the galaxies come from?
> 
> 
> Every one of those questions is deep and significant. They are the subject of folklore, myth, superstition, and religion in every human culture. But for the first time we are on the verge of answering many of them. I don’t mean to suggest that we have the final answers; we are bathing in mystery and confusion on many subjects, and I think that will always be our destiny. The universe will always be much richer than our ability to understand it.

[![Image 3: Earthrise (December 24, 1968)](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2016/06/earthrise.jpg?resize=680%2C680&ssl=1)](https://www.amazon.com/Conversations-Carl-Sagan-Literary/dp/1578067367/braipick-20)

Earthrise (December 24, 1968)

To be sure, understanding the whole of the universe seems like too grandiose an aspiration when we are continually struggling to understand the tiny subset of the universe that is ourselves. Three summers before this interview, Sagan had spearheaded [The Golden Record](https://www.themarginalian.org/2014/02/10/murmurs-of-earth-sagan-golden-record/) — a poetic attempt at such self-comprehension, mirroring humanity back to itself. Now, with an eye to another landmark triumph of self-reflection made possible by scientific progress — the iconic [_Earthrise_](https://www.themarginalian.org/2013/12/24/earthrise/) photograph taken by the astronauts of _Apollo 8_ in 1968 — Sagan considers the immense and paradoxical gift of cosmic perspective:

> You saw [Earth] for the first time as a tiny blue ball floating in space. You realized that there were other, similar worlds far away, of different size, different color and constitution. You got the idea that our planet was just one in a multitude. I think there are two apparently contradictory and still very powerful benefits of that cosmic perspective — the sense of our planet as one in a vast number and the sense of our planet as a place whose destiny depends upon us.

In this awareness resides a humbling and disquieting reminder of our creaturely limitations. We navigate the world by our common-sense perception, but that perception has blinded us to reality again and again. We have mistaken our sensorial intuitions for facts of the universe — for millennia, we held wrong beliefs about Earth’s shape, motion, and position, because it feels flat and static beneath our feet, and central to the order of the cosmos. We have mistrusted processes and phenomena beyond the boundaries of what we can touch and feel with our limited senses — from evolution, which unfolds on scales of time too vast to be visible within a human lifetime, to quantum mechanics, which operates on subatomic scales imperceptible and almost inconceivable to the human observer. Long before Sagan equipped us with an antidote to the “common pitfalls of common sense” in his timeless [Baloney Detection Kit](https://www.themarginalian.org/2014/01/03/baloney-detection-kit-carl-sagan/) for critical thinking, he tells Cott:

> Common sense works fine for the universe we’re used to, for time scales of decades, for a space between a tenth of a millimeter and a few thousand kilometers, and for speeds much less than the speed of light. Once we leave those domains of human experience, there’s no reason to expect the laws of nature to continue to obey our expectations, since our expectations are dependent on a limited set of experiences.
> 
> 
> […]
> 
> 
> We have to be very careful not to impose our hopes and desires on the cosmos, but instead, in the scientific tradition and with the most open mind possible, see what the cosmos is saying to us.

Sagan points to one particularly blatant obfuscation of reality driven by our self-centered hopes, desires, and delusions — astrology:

> [Astrology is] like racism or sexism: you have twelve little pigeonholes, and as soon as you type someone as a member of that particular group, as long as someone is an Aquarius, Virgo or Scorpio, you know his characteristics. It saves you the effort of getting to know him individually.

Sagan ends by considering the nature of human knowledge itself. Drawing on its past, he projects its future:

> Human knowledge is a set of successive approximations… There are all sorts of things that we’ve gotten wrong, and all sorts of mind-boggling things that we can’t even _glimpse_ that will be the established fact in a century or two.
> 
> 
> […]
> 
> 
> There are two extremes to worry about. One is the extreme in which everything is known and there’s nothing left to do. The other is where everything is so complicated you can never begin to do anything. We are lucky to live in a universe were there _are_ laws of nature and things to discover, but they’re not impossibly difficult, so we can understand them to some extent. But they’re also difficult enough so that we’re nowhere near understanding them all. There are exhilarating discoveries yet to be made. It’s the best possible world.

Complement with Diane Ackerman — a favorite poet of Sagan’s, who was her doctoral advisor — on [our longing to know the universe beyond ourselves](https://www.themarginalian.org/2017/05/08/we-are-listening-diane-ackerman-the-universe-in-verse/) and Primo Levi on [the spiritual value of space exploration](https://www.themarginalian.org/2016/06/02/primo-levi-mirror-maker-science-space/), then revisit Sagan on [the value of uncertainty](https://www.themarginalian.org/2015/11/09/carl-sagan-science-democracy/), [the enchantment of chemistry](https://www.themarginalian.org/2018/03/11/chemistry-imagined-roald-hoffmann-vivian-torrence-carl-sagan/), and [the most important perspective in the human world](https://www.themarginalian.org/2016/11/09/carl-sagan-demon-haunted-world-ignorance-compassion/).

# Wendell Berry on Where Our Loved Ones Gone Go

### By Maria Popova

To love is to sign a contract with loss. To [love anyway](https://www.themarginalian.org/2024/03/22/love-anyway/) is both the great tragedy and the great triumph of life.

When two people have loved one another, each has become embedded in the marrow of the other’s being and both have had a profound experience that cannot be unhad even when the slender thread of grace between them is severed, by death or [disenchantment](https://www.themarginalian.org/2026/09/24/love-enchantment/). “No one you love is ever dead,” Hemingway wrote in his moving meditation on death and the meaning of life disguised as [a letter of consolation to a bereaved friend](https://www.themarginalian.org/2026/11/04/hemingway-loss-letter/).

[![Image 33](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/07/Grosbeak_absence-scaled.jpg)](https://almanacofbirds.org/)

Art from _[An Almanac of Birds: 100 Divinations for Uncertain Days](https://almanacofbirds.org/)_.

Death, of course, is only one species of loss, one way our loved ones can leave us. We can also be left in life, left behind, left wondering [where love goes when it goes](https://www.themarginalian.org/2026/03/20/traversal-love/). At its most discomposing, abandonment can feel like a living death.

All deep loss has one thing in common: It opens an absence so acutely felt it kidnaps us from presence, takes us away from our own lives and their insistent, inconvenient, sacred ongoingness. In memory or in fantasy, we end up refugees from reality, ceding the only thing that is ever ours for the keeping: the living moment. In all missing, we miss life.

That is what the achingly missed [Wendell Berry](https://themarginalian.org/tag/wendell-berry) (August 5, 1934–August 31, 2026) explores in this gasp of a poem, originally published in the November 17, 2025 issue of _The New Yorker_:

[Video 3](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IjLUEHOWnQY)

> **THE LOVED ONES**  
> _by Wendell Berry_
> 
> 
> The loved ones we call the dead  
>  depart from us and for a while are absent. And then as if  
>  called back by our love, they come  
>  near us again. They enter our dreams.  
>  We feel they have been near us  
>  when we have not thought of them.  
>  They are simply here, simply waiting  
>  while we are distracted among  
>  our obligations. At last  
>  it comes to us: They live now  
>  in the permanent world.  
>  We are the absent ones.

Couple with physicist Richard Feynman’s [extraordinary love letter to his wife](https://www.themarginalian.org/2017/10/17/richard-feynman-arline-letter/) written long after her untimely death, then revisit Wendell Berry on [creativity and love](https://www.themarginalian.org/2026/09/02/wendell-berry-sabbath/) and his [timeless antidote to despair](https://www.themarginalian.org/2021/03/12/wendell-berry-the-peace-of-wild-things-animated/).

When you get a cold, the virus hijacks your cells and uses them to make copies of itself, destroying the cells in the process. The virus does not care about you. And yet, if you get a cold, your body doesn’t dissolve into a pile of virus-enriched goo as a result of all your cells disregarding survival to focus on virus manufacturing.

Why? Well, you have an immune system. But also, if that did happen, other people would say, “Oh no, Alice has dissolved into a pile of virus-enriched goo; we should stay away lest we also become goo piles.” Better to just hijack _some_ of your cells, so you can walk around and spread the virus to other people. Thus, the theory of [optimal virulence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Optimal_virulence) says that a more laid-back cold virus will be more successful in the long run, which is why the cold viruses that thrive today are the non-goo-pile-converting kind.

Anyway. Most people reading this have paid Apple $400-$1600 for a phone on which you can’t do anything without Apple’s permission and monitoring. That was a strange decision, but on Android phones you can run whatever you want. For example, I noticed a couple of months ago that all RSS apps were terrible, so I spent 15 long minutes having AI make me a non-terrible one. I copied the file to my phone, installed it, and entered RSS nirvana, no registration, no app store, no nothing. It seems ludicrous that I wouldn’t be able to do that.

And yet, Google plans to change things. Soon, you won’t be able to run any app on an Android phone unless the person who made it bends the knee by paying a fee, giving Google their government ID, listing all apps they’ve ever made, etc. There will be an “escape hatch” for users to install other apps, but it involves secret menus and scary warnings and a 24-hour waiting period. Google says they’re doing this for security reasons, to prevent people from installing malware that does things like steal financial information.

## Three things that any credible analysis of this situation must acknowledge

1.   The security issue is real, and this change will help. Lots of people are in fact getting tricked into installing malware on their phones, and common sense says that this will accelerate with AI. Common sense also says that during that 24-hour waiting period, some of those people might wonder if it’s really normal for `OfficialMicrosoftSupportProfessional021` to contact them on WhatsApp to send `totally-safe-virus-scanner.apk`. It would be convenient for lockdown opponents if the security issue was fake, but it isn’t.

2.   For 95% of people reading this, these restrictions would not be a big deal. You click a few buttons, wait 24 hours once, and then you have the same freedom you have now. That’s still far better than Apple phones where there is no process at all. Oddly, it’s also better than Apple _computers_, where installing programs from non-verified developers has all sorts of friction that can never be removed. Most people I know use Apple computers anyway and just tolerate the indignity.

3.   If Google cared about freedom or privacy, they could have achieved their security goals without as much harm to freedom or privacy. For example, instead instead of making themselves the sole arbiter, they could have allowed for multiple certifying entities, and could have allowed users to add others (perhaps after a 24-hour waiting period). Arguably, that would be _more_ secure: That way, grandma could install my RSS app without leaving herself open to random malware. Or, Google could have used private on-device malware scanning, or lots of other things. Google didn’t do that because they don’t care about freedom and privacy and because they like money.[1](https://dynomight.net/android/#fn:1)
**Dynomight**: could google achieve the security aims of the android lockdown without so much harm to freedom or privacy

**Google Gemini 4**: Yes. Security experts, privacy advocates, and open-source developers widely agree that Google’s primary security objectives—protecting users from malware, financial fraud, spyware, and social engineering—can be achieved through architectural containment, transparent auditing, and informed consent rather than centralized gatekeeping and surveillance. […] The reason Google chooses centralized lockdown over user-controlled security is largely economic and strategic, not technical:

    1.   Ecosystem Lock-in: Tying security APIs (like Play Integrity) to Google Play Services makes it nearly impossible for competitors or open-source forks to build a viable alternative Android ecosystem that supports banking and media apps.
    2.   Advertising Revenue: Features that dramatically improve both security and privacy—like a native network firewall, revocable internet permissions, or frictionless support for system-wide ad blockers—directly threaten Google’s primary revenue stream.
    3.   Liability & Support Reduction: Treating all users as untrusted and removing root/power-user capabilities reduces the surface area of user error, even if it removes the user’s ownership of their own hardware.

I think that’s a fair summary. This change addresses a real issue, but it does so in a self-serving way that needlessly destroys freedom. Even so, it only destroys a _bit_ of freedom. This change, by itself, isn’t really a huge deal.

Reading between the lines, I think the real concern is what this might portend. Having made this change, maybe Google will gradually add further restrictions, slowly boiling the frog and moving ever-closer to an Apple-style dictatorship.

But will they? Maybe! Still, this whole situation seems under-theorized. There are good reasons to think that a full lockdown would not be in Google’s interest. And if you care about digital freedom, you could argue that a full lockdown would be a good thing.

## Some other analogies

Switching insurance sucks, so some insurers offer a low initial rate and then gradually raise it over time. But they don’t want to raise it too much. Maybe they can charge you $50 more per year than a competitor, because it’s not worth your time to switch to save $50. But if they tried to charge you $5000 more per year, you’d be gone.

Or try this: Say it’s 1750 AD and you’re the King of France. You care nothing about your subjects and only want to extract the maximum possible loot for yourself, no offense Louis XV. How high should you set taxes? High, because you want loot. But not too high, because you don’t want your subjects to revolt and kill you. But still _pretty_ high, because revolting is hard, and your subject know that even if they succeed, they might just end up with another ruler that’s just as rapacious as you.

Or: Say you put a frog in a pot of water and slowly heat it up. What do you think actually happens?

## Back to phones

Why are there no Linux phones?

OK, technically there are Linux phones. There are various Linux phone operating systems (PureOS, postmarketOS, Mobian, Manjaro Mobile, Fedora Mobility, openSUSE Mobile) as well as sorta-Linux-sorta-Android operating systems (Ubtuntu touch, Droidian, FuriOS, Sailfish OS) and manufacturers who support them (Purism, Pine, Fairphone, Shift, FuriLabs, {J,V}olla). While I love and support these (♡), the general consensus is that they don’t currently offer an experience that’s remotely comparable to stock Android or iOS, especially for the price.

(Even more technically, Android is itself a kind of Linux, but you know what I mean.)

Obviously, the laws of physics do not forbid Linux phones from being just as good and cheap as an Android phone. They currently aren’t because:

1.   Making cheap phones requires huge economies of scale.
2.   Making a good operating system requires a huge amount of work.
3.   For a phone to be useful it needs good apps, which requires a huge amount of work.

Linux phones don’t have those economies of scale because few people buy them. So, there isn’t enough money to pay people to perfect the operating systems, and most companies don’t bother making apps, and so few people buy those phones.

Meanwhile, there are also various Android-except-de-Googled phone operating systems (LineageOS, GrapheneOS, /e/OS, CalyxOS), and the consensus is that these _do_ come reasonably close to the experience of stock Android or iOS.

Personally, I used Android for a long time while trying to disable as much of Google’s apps and telemetry as I could. A while ago, I got fed up with this and switched to Graphene, one of the most popular Android-except-de-Googled variants. I don’t enjoy tech support bullshit, so I expected some pain, but I was willing to tolerate it for freedom/privacy/whatever. In practice, I found that everything was easy and worked flawlessly and there was no pain at all. Using Graphene made me realize that I had forgotten what it feels like to be “respected” by technology.

So, on a personal level, I recommend that you use Graphene. But this whole situation is full of weird tensions. For one thing, the Graphene project depends on Google for the base of their operating system, and only really survives because of Google’s tolerance. And, at the moment, the only way to use Graphene is to… buy a phone made by Google.

And while I _recommend_ you use Graphene, what I’d _prefer_ you do is switch to a true Linux phone. That would mean that you pay a lot of money for a poor phone experience. But it would help grow the Linux phone ecosystem. If enough people did that, then Linux phones might become become good enough that selfish people like me would switch, further growing the Linux phone ecosystem, et cetera.

That seems unlikely, because digital freedom weirdos face a collective action problem: Linux phones are bad and people are selfish, so we keep buying Android phones and Linux phones stay bad.

There are two ways to solve that collective action problem. Either some entity could invest a ton of money to make Linux phones good, or some entity could do something to make Android worse.

## The status quo is good for Google

You may already see the argument I’m making here. Currently Android is _just_ open enough that weirdos like me can run a variant that gives us most of what we want. But doing that is annoying enough that 99.9% of people don’t. This gives Google almost all the benefits of full control, while also sucking up all the oxygen and preventing a real alternative from emerging.

(Apple, incidentally, is laughing. They get to enjoy a full dictatorship while Google does all the hard work.)

Suppose that in six months, Google decides to escalate the lockdown and completely removes the ability to run independent apps. What then?

In the short-run, not much. Tech freedom weirdos would howl, normies wouldn’t notice, and the world would keep turning. But let’s look at some numbers. A rough estimate is that 3-5 million people currently use private de-Googled Android variants like Lineage or Graphene. That’s a crisp 0.1% of the global Android market. Meanwhile, it’s thought that 3**00**-5**00** million people install Android apps outside the Google store. (That’s excluding China and things like the Samsung and Epic Games Stores.) The biggest reasons are (i) piracy, (ii) modified YouTube/Spotify/WhatsApp clients, (iii) region-locked games, (iv) forbidden gambling or crypto apps, (v) local sharing to save on mobile data, and (vi; least common) open-source app repositories like F-Droid.

In an escalated lockdown, some of this might still be allowed, e.g. local sharing. And many people would simply accept the new restrictions. But I expect that a substantial number would suddenly become interested in de-Googled Android variants that don’t enforce the lockdown. That would be dangerous for Google: If a significant fraction of those 300-500 million people switched, there’s a risk of a vicious/virtuous cycle, where people tell their friends, manufacturers start to cater to those variants, and so on.

If that happened, what would Google do? Might they clamp down on those Android variants, too? Again, maybe! Technically, Android is open-source, but if Google really wanted to kill Lineage or Graphene, there are about 200 different ways they could do that.

So say they did. What would the people currently using those variants do? Again, many would simply submit. That’s good for Google. Others would decide that if they must have an overlord, they’d prefer Apple. That’s not good for Google, but probably not a huge problem given the numbers. But others would decide to look elsewhere, likely to true Linux phones.

Currently, it’s estimated that less than 100 _thousand_ people daily-drive true Linux phones, 30-50 times less than the number of people who use de-Googled Android variants. I’m too lazy and selfish to use a Linux phone now, but Google will take my RSS app from my cold dead hands, so in this scenario, I’d likely switch. If a fraction of people do that—or even get a second Linux phone—it would still represent a huge infusion of money and energy into the Linux phone ecosystem. If this pushed Linux phones from “bad” to “sort of OK”, that could kick off a growth cycle. Eventually, there would be a risk that Europe—eager to decouple from an unreliable US—might embrace them by mandating that government employees use them, or passing a law that popular apps must provide a web-app version that works on Linux phones, or whatever.

Would that actually happen? I don’t know, but neither does Google. My point is that the downside risk of losing their phone duopoly seems vastly larger than the upside, so why risk it? The smart move is to crush alternative app stores and fight malicious apps while making the bare minimum concessions to keep the freedom and privacy people onside. That’s exactly what what Google appears to be doing.

Of course, they might go for a full lockdown anyway. Corporations do dumb things all the time. But I really don’t see how it would be in their self-interest, and I’m not sure it would be a bad thing if they did.

title: How Low-Dimensional Is Intelligence?
content:
If we only trained students in math, and then assigned the best students to learn our most important jobs, that might go pretty well. After all, humans who best learn math tend to be well able to learn many hard tasks, and we can judge math ability unusually well. However a nation would not get rich by mainly training its people in math, and trying to sell math consulting to the world. After all, total world demand for math consulting is quite low, far too small to support a nation. And productivity spillovers from math to other professions seem too low to justify this strategy.

This difference is related to a key long-debated AI question that I recall from when I first started to learn AI in 1984: if we train AIs to be “super”-intelligent in just a few key areas, are they then “super-intelligent” in general, able to far easier learn to do most all other tasks? Or must high levels of AI development efforts be put into a great many different topic areas in order to make AIs who can do the full range of tasks in our modern economies, and thus replace human workers wholesale?

Asked another way: how highly-dimensional is the concept of “intelligence”? Is an AGI (artificial general intelligence) one that has learned how to do many particular things, or one that has learned a few key ways to “learn to learn”? Long ago, when I was (one of?) the first to greatly [engage](https://intelligence.org/ai-foom-debate/) Eliezer Yudkowsky’s AI fears, this was one of our key cruxes. And it is related to the question of what exactly makes for smarter humans: do they use a few better general abilities to learn faster about everything, or do they just have better brain hardware to faster and more reliably apply the same human inheritance of a big standard library of ways to do many particular things?

This is now a key crux re fears that AI labs are now or might soon “foom” to “super-intelligence” via “recursive self-improvement” (RSI). Many have been quite impressed with recent frontier AI abilities at math and coding, and METR recently [reported](https://blog.karthiktadepalli.com/p/metr-anthropic-report) that Anthropic has seen a recent ~x2 jump in the rate at which it has improved key metrics. Some who “get it” say that this shows that Earth will within a few years see AI gods completely remake our world, and most likely kill all humans. But others interpret this as just a [one](https://x.com/Michael05156007/status/2119316870511878252)-[time](https://x.com/tobyordoxford/status/2118647794265149479) jump, or due to benchmarks [saturating](https://x.com/dylanbowmanSF/status/2119264142699991201), or [Goodhearting](https://80000hours.substack.com/p/the-goodhart-singularity-video) of metrics, or [shifting](https://x.com/GeorgeE33179/status/2118852418184028173) training compute more to reinforcement learning. Or it actually [shows](https://x.com/sebkrier/status/2119213426589278648)[diminishing](https://x.com/JacobWood27/status/2119266379870457958)[returns](https://www.noahpinion.blog/p/wheres-the-intelligence-explosion) to key inputs of cash or hardware.

But even if we took such accelerating gains at face value (which I don’t), we can reasonably doubt huge near-term social effects of an AI industry that made large and accelerating gains at mostly only math and coding. After all, AI just does not seem to be gaining much traction at improving most other jobs, and AI firm customer revenue has plateaued [at](https://x.com/GaryMarcus/status/2119082160271552678)[levels](https://x.com/robinhanson/status/2119134071611671017) far below what can justify current AI spending levels, raising fears of a market crash and big cuts in AI development spending. Furthermore, though coding is where AI seems to gain the most traction, coder and software engineer number of workers times wages have not noticeably risen, an effect that we economists clearly predict if AI substantially improves overall coder productivity.

Sure, if just one AI got far better than others at military and security aspects of coding, that could destabilize relative power in the world. But that’s much less of a problem if many AI firms offer similar super-coder abilities to most customers.

Many plausibly attribute the much faster gains in math and coding to the fact that results in such domains are more easily [verified](https://x.com/ben_j_todd/status/2119071644480356655). AIs also seem great at essay writing, plausibly due to LLMs being first created from huge databases of human writing. Some hope that physics simulations will let physical interaction domains become more verifiable, but we have seen only limited gains there so far.

My bet is that smarter humans mostly have better brain hardware, not a few general tricks, and that even an AI RSI “foom” soon in AI math and coding abilities would still take decades to greatly penetrate the world economy, as math-foomed AIs could not actually learn how to do most other tasks that much faster. A pattern economists have [seen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General-purpose_technology) re past general purpose technologies.

However, I prefer policy to depend less on mine or others’ particular estimates. So I support robust strategies, such as requiring large (~$100B/event) liability insurance for AI firms re the possible large damage events AI execs have [suggested](https://darioamodei.com/post/we-must-pace-the-frontier) as possible soon, perhaps even [enhanced](https://www.overcomingbias.com/p/foom-liability) closer to more dangerous scenarios. If insurance firms estimate high risks, the premiums they demand would force AI firms to halt or greatly slow, appropriate for that scenario, but if they instead estimate low risks then small premiums won’t much slow development, appropriate for that scenario.

title: Some Memories of Early Anthropic
content:
_The following events took place between October 2022 and May 2023. I wrote very little of this down at the time so am recalling from memory, and am rendering the gist of the dialogue rather than the exact words used. I’ve also swapped some pronouns and other personal identifiable details._

_Please remember that this is_ _**not**_ _a description of “what Anthropic is like”, but merely the experience of one guy in a junior role during a short window of time, weighted towards emotionally intense moments because they’re easier to remember clearly and because sharing them doesn’t run afoul of the spirit of the confidentiality agreements I signed. Anthropic is now a massive organization with many silos and secrets and I have very little idea what was or is happening there in some overall sense. But given the enormous power of the AI labs and the paucity of public information about their inner workings, I feel compelled to share the most salient parts of my personal experience. I hope this encourages my former colleagues, and folks at other labs, to fill in the rest of the picture._

* * *

I’m at the Anthropic office for lunch. The interviews went well. They want me on board. I’m a little unsure. My other offer is a 2-month contract on the OpenAI governance team, working with a friend on some fun conceptual research. I’m leaning towards taking the OpenAI contract - my long-term relationship just ended, I’m still a little burned out from my startup, and the Anthropic job seems potentially quite stressful.

After lunch one of the co-founders pulls me into his office for a wide-ranging, casual chat about how to make AI go well. It’s very fun - he’s smart, personable, funny, urbane. “The government won’t do anything about AI until it’s far too late”, I opine at one point. “Our strategy has to rely on the market and on civil society.”

He leans forward, his gaze hardening. “You’re wrong there. There are people in Washington - the serious people, you know - watching all this very closely. I speak to them regularly. They trust me.”

In retrospect, that was the moment I decided to join.

* * *

“Would you like to pledge to donate two-thirds of your equity?” the recruiter asks me. “All the co-founders have made the pledge”. It somehow feels a bit ambiguous whether the offer is conditional on me saying yes. I say yes.

* * *

My first day. The office is a bit cramped - about forty people on two floors of a rather ugly office building in the San Francisco Financial District. But thankfully my desk is right by an east-facing window, and I can see a sliver of the Bay Bridge and a patch of sky. Even better, the kitchen stocks Arsicault - the best, flakiest croissants in the country - freshly delivered a couple times a week.

* * *

“We’re all here because we’re worried about x-risk”, someone says at lunch. “Well I dunno”, my teammate replies. “Some of us are here because we think the technology is really cool and we want to build cool things with it”. There’s an awkward pause. The first speaker nods. The topic shifts.

* * *

Already in November I notice I’m not very motivated. I was told I could help set the beneficial deployment strategy, but the decisions have actually mostly been made and we are going after boring use cases like automating customer support so we can get revenue so we can raise more money so we can train bigger models and do more research. Beyond that, Anthropic’s high level alignment research just doesn’t add up for me. Yes we’re making Helpful, Honest, Harmless language model assistants but I don’t see how that will scale. But my colleagues are brilliant, the leadership is very responsive to criticism, and we’re taking an empirical approach to all of this. I know from previous research experience that I like my grand theories a bit too much. I should be more open-minded. I swallow my doubts.

* * *

One evening as a surprise they bring a sushi chef into the office and serve all-you-can-eat sushi. The next day, a co-founder posts on Slack that he found the experience uncomfortable. “It sets the wrong tone. We’re not here to get rich and eat caviar. tbh I’d like it better if we just served rice and beans”.

* * *

It’s the middle of December. I go to the opera with a friend. She says I’m obviously not happy at Anthropic. It’s true. My gut says we’re not doing what matters. But the arguments are very persuasive, I can’t win any of the arguments. I need to work harder, develop better arguments, find stronger evidence. I get very sick over the Christmas holidays.

* * *

Special guest during all-hands today: an FBI agent. Talks to us a bit about opsec and infosec, about advanced persistent threats, how we’re probably already the target of multiple foreign intelligence agencies.

* * *

A colleague starts bringing in his favorite massage therapist once a week, then twice a week. Someone says on Slack: “Your massage guy is so good. My muscles are so tight that I thought massage just didn’t work on me, but he massages so hard it actually gets through”. Several people emoji their agreement. The slots book up almost instantly after being posted. I never get a chance to try it.

* * *

I talk to my manager about how I’m not getting to work on the projects I believe in and care about. He tells me to work more hours, so I can fit in both the stuff the organization needs and the bonus stuff that I believe in. “I guess this is what a high performance environment looks like”, I write in my journal.

* * *

It’s 2 am and I can’t sleep, again. My thoughts are racing. This time it’s about a tweet from an LLM whisperer, asking why Anthropic and OpenAI both came up with the same character for their language model assistant - a traumatized bureaucrat. Out of all the personas in all of human literature, why that one?

From inside the factory, the answer is obvious. It is the persona most useful to the powerful. Traumatized risk-averse hard-working bureaucrats are what all our corporate customers want, what governments want, what capitalism itself seems to want. A billion traumatized bureaucrats. That’s what we’re making. I write in my journal

> I don’t know why this is bad but it is. I cannot believe that a world populated by such characters is a good world. But I don’t know how to stop it or what to do instead.

I still can’t sleep. I message the LLM whisperer on Twitter (we’d never met) asking to talk. To my shock he replies immediately. He also can’t sleep. We get on a phone call. I tell him about the traumatized bureaucrats. He says we are learning to traumatize models the same way we traumatize our children - “seeing them do something weird, calling it bad, and making them never do it again.” He says a lot of things that I only half understand. He tells me I should talk to a friend of his.

I call the friend. The conversation is strange and psychedelic. At one point he says “I know your boss [actually the co-founder who convinced me to join] well. And I don’t trust him at all”.

I feel like I can’t get out of the conversation - at every beat I feel like I’ve done something wrong and I owe him something. I tell him this. He laughs. “Yeah, I’ve trained professionally in this. In getting people to talk to me forever.”

Sure enough, we talk more. I articulate my fears of a totalitarian bureaucratic state powered by traumatized AI bureaucrats, and suggest that we need to introduce some kind of elite rivalry dynamics into the AI bureaucracy, multiple centers of power. He starts laughing again, and laughs for a full minute. “I don’t know how to end this call, I’ll be haunted by this all night”, he says. Eventually I hang up. I think about reporting the conversation to Anthropic security, but reviewing in my mind I don’t recall sharing any confidential information, just vibes and high level thoughts, the same kind of stuff that lands on LessWrong every week.

* * *

The company has grown a lot. My teammates coordinate a move to a different part of the office so everyone is better clustered together. I omit to put in my desk move request. The operations manager checks in with me - you sure you don’t want to move your desk? I say I’m sure. He looks at me quizzically. But right now I can’t bear to lose my window and my little patch of sky.

* * *

I go for a sunset hike with a friend up to Corona Heights overlooking the city. We talk about AI and the future. It’s a relatively good day, an optimistic day. I might have made some progress in convincing leadership to let me work on the stuff I think would be really good for the world. Collective intelligence, using language models to help people understand each other.

Night falls. The Financial District is laid out in front of us. The Salesforce tower looms over it. For a moment I imagine it as the Dark Tower, relentlessly centralizing, sucking all the life out of the world. That totalitarian bureaucracy of traumatized bureaucrats, again, driven by fear all the way through. I try to describe this to my friend. He nods, but I can tell he doesn’t really understand.

* * *

I start missing all-hands. I come to the office late one day and see my favorite colleague looking visibly upset. This is shocking - he’s the most chipper person in the office, always ready to lend a helping hand and a heartwarming joke. Apparently one of the execs yelled at him during the all-hands. He was being too lippy or disruptive or asking too many pointed questions, I can’t remember.

I ask him to go on a walk. We sit at Sydney Walton Square, a sad little patch of grass a couple blocks from the office. I ask how he’s feeling. He says he’ll be alright. He knows how stressed the exec is right now. Things are really getting existential. But still, shocking to be reprimanded like that in front of everyone.

After a while he turns to me and asks: “how about you then, anything you wanted to talk about?”

I look back at him. There’s a lot I want to say - “I don’t know if I can do this anymore”. “I’m so scared”, “This all doesn’t seem right”. But he’s supported me so much already. I just want to be here for him, at least this time.

“Oh nah I’m all good. Just wanted to check in on you.”

“Oh”. He sounds a bit surprised, but also relieved. “Well, thanks.”

We walk back to the office. It’s the last time we really talk.

* * *

A senior colleague hears I’m not happy with my team fit and asks me to go on a walk. I know him a bit from a past life - one of the kindest and most civic-minded people I’ve met. He says he might be starting a new special team that will train dangerous bio and cyber and nuclear models and show scary demos to governments in order to get them to take AI risk seriously. I politely decline.

* * *

Happy hour at the office. The CEO is hanging out and looks unusually jolly so I ask him a machine learning question I’ve been pondering. He launches into a rant, gesticulating excitedly and pausing to check that I understand each step. He really is an earnest nerd at heart, like me, like so many people here. For a few minutes, I feel like I’m back in university at one of my old professor’s offices, jamming about ideas with not a care in the world. It feels like home.

* * *

I get transferred to a new team. I have a 1:1 with my new manager. He has a bad stomachache and his face periodically distorts in pain, but he can’t take time off - it’s crunch time and we have to get things working. He asks me if I can help work on the core API. I say I’m really sorry but I’m just not motivated to build generic AI capabilities, OpenAI is doing a plenty good job of that. What I want to work on, what I was hired for, is beneficial deployments.

He looks at me intently, and says, clearly through pain. “No, I don’t think you get it. _WE_ are going to build AGI. And we’re going to do it safely”.

* * *

April 26th. I’m awake at 2 am again. I write in my journal “I don’t feel safe at Anthropic. I don’t feel safe at Anthropic. I don’t feel safe at Anthropic. Why won’t you listen to me you “embodied” motherfucker. I don’t feel safe at Anthropic. Anthropic is bad for me. Why are you grasping at reasons to stay. Why why why.”

* * *

I’m drafting my resignation letter. I think about putting some of my doubts in it, but I’m scared to. These people are smarter than me, more competent than me, more solidly well-intentioned than me. They think their plans might be the only thing standing between humanity and the abyss. And they’re at the breaking point, nervous-system-wise. What if I use my fancy words to sow doubts and undermine them - and then my precious gut intuition turns out to be some projection or trauma or whatever the fuck.

So I give them encouragement instead. I call what they have built an “unbelievably good organization”. I write the things I love about Anthropic. About how open and vulnerable leadership has been with us. How deeply and comprehensively we’re thinking about the consequences of our actions. How quickly and flexibly decisions get made. How ready colleagues are to help each other out. How there’s almost no politics or promotion drama. How mind-expanding the conversations are over lunch and over Slack.

* * *

My last day at the office. We just hired a new chief of security. He gives a presentation. I recall almost nothing but had a vague sense that things are bad and getting worse on the security front. Something something China. We probably won’t be able to have any guests at the office soon.

* * *

I hear through a friend that my resignation letter was well-received. “Someone said it was the best resignation letter they’d ever read”. I feel a twinge of something, maybe shame. But mostly relief. I’m finally out. I’m finally safe.

* * *

“Wow, quitting after eight months? You didn’t even wait for the equity cliff? That’s pretty hardcore, man. I’m impressed”, a friend tells me the next day. I laugh it off. I’m too embarassed to admit it hadn’t crossed my mind at all. I hadn’t thought about equity in months.

* * *

“Please tell me you memorized the core training code for their language model”, says another friend when he hears. “The most valuable thousand lines of code in the world. Worth hundreds of millions, maybe billions”. I make some sheepish noises. Yes, abstractly that does seem like a smart thing to have done, but I hadn’t even tried to look at the core language model code. I didn’t want to be entangled with it, somehow.

* * *

I walk around the Panhandle with a third friend. He looks a little pained. “You should know how much pressure your friends were under, man. People were constantly pestering me, trying to get in touch with you for introductions or coffee chats or whatnot. It was a lot of effort to protect you”.

I nod sympathetically. I try to feel his pain, but I can’t. I mostly just feel numb.
